headline: Morocco Makes History With First Female Prime Minister
meta_description: King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as Morocco's first woman prime minister, making her the third in the Arab world.
summary_short: Morocco appointed its first female prime minister on September 29, joining Tunisia in a regional shift toward women in top leadership roles.
body:
On September 29, King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as Morocco's prime minister, making the 50-year-old urban planner the first woman to lead the government in the kingdom's history and only the third woman to serve as prime minister across the Arab world. In a televised address following her appointment, El Mansouri spoke directly to the significance of the moment: "For the first time in our country's history, a woman is taking on the responsibility of leading the government. This is a source of pride not only for me but for all Moroccan women." Her path to the top reflects decades of progressive public service. Born in Marrakesh in 1976, El Mansouri studied law in France and New York before entering local politics in 2009, when she became the first woman elected mayor of Marrakesh at age 33. In 2021, she moved to national government as Minister of National Spatial Planning, Urban Development, Housing and Urban Policy—a role that put her in charge of rehousing tens of thousands of people displaced by the devastating 2023 Al Haouz earthquake in the High Atlas mountains.

El Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party won 97 of 395 seats in September's elections, requiring her to build a coalition to govern. The timing places her at the helm during Morocco's preparation for the 2030 FIFA World Cup, which the country will co-host with Portugal and Spain—a moment that brings both significant infrastructure investment and international scrutiny. Her background in urban development and earthquake recovery makes her well-positioned for the challenge ahead. She joins Tunisia's Sara Zaafarani, appointed in March 2025, as the Arab world's current female prime ministers—a change that seemed far less likely just a decade ago.
